title: Peanut Sauce
author: Zoe Adjei
desc: Her stated childhood favourite — chalé sauce and stock simmered, peanut butter dissolved in gradually, then blended and left to infuse up to two hours.
longDesc: This is groundnut soup turned into a sauce, and the author calls it her ultimate childhood comfort food. Onion is sautéed, the spices and aromatics go in, then half a litre each of uncooked chalé sauce and vegetable stock, simmered fifteen to twenty minutes. Peanut butter is added gradually until dissolved, the whole thing is blended smooth, and then eight green kpakpo shito chillies go in for a final simmer of thirty minutes or more. Her note is that she often leaves it up to two hours so the flavours really infuse, but thirty to forty minutes is good enough.
ingredients: 5 cm piece fresh root ginger, grated — unpeeled if organic
steps: Heat the groundnut oil and sauté the onion about 2 minutes.
Add the chilli powder, curry powder, garlic, ginger, pierced scotch bonnet, crushed peanuts, salt and black pepper.
Add the uncooked chalé sauce and the vegetable stock.
Add the peanut butter gradually, until dissolved.
Add the green kpakpo shito chillies.
Simmer 30 minutes or more — up to 2 hours for a fuller flavour.
chefTips: Her own timing note is the useful one: she often leaves it simmering up to two hours so the flavours really infuse, but thirty to forty minutes is good enough. Both are her words.
Peanut butter gradually until dissolved, as in every groundnut preparation. It will not come back together if you let it clump.
Blend AFTER the peanut butter has dissolved and BEFORE the kpakpo shito goes in. The whole chillies are meant to stay whole and infuse.
Half a litre each of chalé sauce and stock — equal parts, which makes this the most straightforward ratio in her repertoire.
Crushed roasted peanuts go in early with the spices, separately from the peanut butter. Two textures of the same nut, and it matters.
A tablespoon each of extra-hot chilli powder and curry powder is a lot. A second printing of this sauce halves both, so taste as you go.
Vegan as written with vegetable stock, which is worth knowing — few West African sauces this rich are.
commonMistakes: Adding the peanut butter all at once.
Blending after the kpakpo shito has gone in.
Leaving out the crushed peanuts because the peanut butter is already there.
Treating thirty minutes as the maximum rather than the minimum.
Using cooked chalé sauce where uncooked is specified.
sources: Adapted from 'Peanut Sauce', splendidtable.org, 20 July 2017. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'by Zoe Adjonyoh'. CREDIT AS PRINTED: 'Reprinted with permission from Zoe's Ghana Kitchen by Zoe Adjonyoh. Copyright 2017, Mitchell Beazley.' Yield as printed: 'Makes 850-900 ml (about 1½ pints)'. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).
HEADNOTE, verbatim: 'My ultimate childhood comfort food - I absolutely love this sauce!'

Ingredients exactly as printed: 1 tablespoon groundnut oil; 1 onion, finely diced; 1 tablespoon extra-hot chilli powder; 1 tablespoon curry powder; 1 garlic clove, crushed; 5 cm (2 inch) piece fresh root ginger, grated (unpeeled if organic); 1 red Scotch Bonnet chilli, pierced; 3 tablespoons crushed roasted peanuts; 2 teaspoons sea salt; 1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper; 500 ml (18 fl oz) uncooked Chalé Sauce; 500 ml (18 fl oz) good-quality vegetable stock; 100-200g (3½-7 oz) organic peanut butter; 8 green kpakpo shito (cherry) chillies.

METHOD CAVEAT: both fetches returned the method SUMMARISED rather than verbatim. The sequence above — sauté the onion (2 minutes, from the first fetch only), add spices and aromatics, add chalé sauce and stock and simmer 15-20 minutes, add peanut butter gradually until dissolved, blend, add the chillies and simmer '30+ minutes' — is as close to the printed steps as two passes allowed, and the 2-minute onion figure is SINGLE-PASS.
THE AUTHOR'S TIMING NOTE, quoted from the first fetch: 'I often leave the peanut sauce to simmer for up to 2 hours so that the flavours really infuse, but 30-40 minutes is good enough.'

A SECOND PRINTING THAT DISAGREES SUBSTANTIALLY, recorded unreconciled: 'Peanut Sauce', deliciousmagazine.co.uk, byline as printed 'Recipe by Zoe Adjonyoh', 'Modified May 26, 2025', 'Serves 4-8'. SINGLE-PASS AND UNVERIFIED — the second fetch refused to return quantities. As printed there: 1 tbsp groundnut oil; 1 medium onion, finely chopped; ½ tbsp curry powder; ½ tbsp extra-hot chilli powder; 1 garlic clove, crushed; 5cm piece fresh ginger, grated; 1 red scotch bonnet chilli, pierced; 3 tbsp roasted peanuts, crushed; 2 tsp sea salt flakes, crushed; 150ml fresh vegetable stock; 150g peanut butter. Its chalé component is made inline: 400g tin chopped tomatoes; 2 tbsp tomato purée; 1 medium onion; 5cm ginger; 1 red scotch bonnet, deseeded; 1 tbsp chilli flakes; 1 tsp crushed sea salt. Its steps: sauté onion 5-6 minutes; stock 'simmer 15-20 minutes until reduced by half'; chalé added '30-40 minutes'; final simmer 'at least 30 minutes'.

THE DIFFERENCES between the two printings: 500 ml stock and 500 ml chalé sauce here against 150 ml stock and an inline chalé there; 100-200 g peanut butter here against 150 g there; a full tablespoon each of chilli and curry powder here against half a tablespoon there. That is roughly a threefold difference in liquid. NOT AVERAGED.
A FLAG ON THE SECOND PRINTING: its method mentions 'pepper' but its ingredient list contains none. Possible omission, NOT corrected.
The second printing's own tips, as printed: 'Omit the chilli flakes or chilli powder if you want a little less heat.' Make ahead: up to 3 days chilled, or 2 months frozen.
This sauce depends on the chalé sauce at GHA031, whose own two printings also disagree — see GHA032.
storage: 3 days refrigerated, or 2 months frozen, per the author's second printing.
reheating: Gentle heat, loosening with stock or water.
healthBenefits: Peanuts supply monounsaturated fat, niacin, folate and vitamin E.
Vegan as written with vegetable stock.
Ginger, garlic and chilli all contribute documented bioactive compounds.
Good plant protein for a sauce.
culturalNote: Turning groundnut soup into a sauce you keep in the fridge is a diaspora move and a sensible one — the flavour of nkatenkwan without the two-hour pot of chicken. That the author names it her childhood comfort food rather than a traditional dish is the honest framing, and the up-to-two-hours simmer is the bit that connects it back to the soup it came from.
